headline: Appledore Cod on the Slack, Stripers Working the Piscataqua All Day
subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline is plenty when you know which fifteen feet of it holds fish.
body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of coastline and think there's nothing to say. I've got a 20-foot Lund and I fish this stretch like it's a hundred and thirty. The Shoals alone will eat a whole season if you let them, and this week they did exactly that for me — cod on the backside of Appledore before most folks had their coffee, stripers running the Piscataqua all day long because the Gulf of Maine hasn't caught the fever the water south of the Cape has.

That's the story right now. South of Cape Cod stripers have gone nocturnal, hugging bunker schools after dark because the water's too warm to move much in daylight. We don't have that problem up here. The Piscataqua stays cool enough, current-scrubbed enough, that stripers will feed right through the middle of the day if the tide's moving. I had fish Tuesday at 11am off the Memorial Bridge pilings, working the seam where the current split around the pier on a strong outgoing — big bucktails, 2-ounce white, bounced slow along bottom in 25 feet. Two fish over 30 inches, a handful of schoolies mixed in chasing the same current line. Dover Point does the same thing on the right tide — anchor up-current of the point, live mackerel or a chunk of pogy on a fish-finder rig, let it sit in the seam. The full moon this week has been running a stiffer tide than normal, and that stiffer current is exactly what wakes these fish up off the bottom structure.

Hampton Harbor's fishing more like a classic August pattern — stripers pushing through the inlet on the incoming, working the sandbars off Hampton Beach and the flats inside toward the marsh. Best window is the last two hours of the flood into the top, right as bait gets squeezed through the cut. Soft plastics, 4-inch white Slug-Go on a light jighead, or a popper at first light if you want to see it happen. There are cocktail bluefish mixed in there too now, chasing peanut bunker that's been thickening up in the back channels all month — small blues, a pound or two, but they'll hit anything that moves fast, and on a light spinning rod they're more fun than they get credit for. We said a couple weeks back that once the peanut bunker spread out, the back-bay blues would follow — that's exactly what's showing up in Hampton now.

Offshore, the Isles of Shoals are still producing cod, but you have to fish them right. Appledore's back ledges and the water off Duck Island are holding fish in 65 to 85 feet, and the bite window is tight — dead slack tide, either top or bottom, is when they'll come up off bottom and hit. I've been jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of mackerel belly, working it just off the rocks where the structure drops. Missed the slack by twenty minutes on Thursday and the bite shut off like someone flipped a switch. That's the Shoals in August — precise, not generous.

Haddock have pushed further out than the Shoals proper. If you want haddock this time of year you're running to Jeffrey's Ledge, 180 to 220 feet, and that's a different kind of day — bigger boat, bait rigs or jigs worked slow off bottom, and you're looking at a full tide cycle out there to make it worth the run. Worth doing if the weather cooperates, but I wouldn't send a small trailer boat out there without a real weather window. Check the forecast twice.

Mackerel are thinning the way they always do once August water settles in warm. Rye Harbor mornings still produce — I had a dozen in twenty minutes on a mackerel tree off the harbor entrance at first light — but the schools are smaller and more scattered than June. If you want a bait bucket full for stripers or cod, get out there at dawn before the sun gets on the water.

Flounder are the one species I can't give you much on right now. Deep holes in the Piscataqua below the Route 4 bridge still hold a few blackbacks on bloodworms and sandworms, fished on the bottom on the slower stages of the tide, but this isn't peak flounder season and I wouldn't plan a trip around it.

Looking ahead, that full moon current should start easing off over the next few days, which usually settles the Shoals slack-tide bite back into a more predictable window rather than the compressed ten-minute pockets we've had. If the wind stays out of the southwest and light, I'd fish Appledore at first light on the morning slack and be back at the dock with a box of cod before the day boats even clear the harbor. If it swings onshore and kicks up the swell around the Shoals, I'd stay inside and work the Piscataqua current seams instead — that bite doesn't care much what the wind's doing offshore.
